extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, human rights and policy observers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of censorship practices, laws, and their effects in Rwanda since the civil war, describing constitutional provisions, statutory offences, media/education controls, and examples of enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional guarantee of freedom of expression (Article 38)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 38 of the Constitution of Rwanda 2003 guarantees "the freedom of expression and freedom of access to information where it does not prejudice public order, good morals, the protection of the youth and children, the right of every citizen to honour and dignity and protection of personal and family privacy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that although the constitution guarantees these freedoms, in practice the many statutory exceptions and their use by authorities have meant the guarantee has not ensured freedom of speech or expression. The constitution's language is therefore presented alongside real-world limits and enforcement practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional guarantee of freedom of the press (Article 34)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 34 of the Rwandan constitution states that "freedom of the press and freedom of information are recognized and guaranteed by the state".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page explains that despite this textual guarantee, the constitution does not in practice prevent media restrictions; authorities have used laws and licensing to restrict the press. This criterion is presented as aspirational rather than dispositive given enforcement realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions permitting limits on expression (public order, morals, youth protection, honour, privacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution conditions freedom of expression and access to information on not prejudicing public order, good morals, protection of youth and children, honour and dignity, and protection of personal and family privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These broadly phrased exceptions are cited as the legal basis authorities use to curtail speech. The text implies these catch-all categories enable wide discretion in enforcement and may be invoked to justify restrictions on critical political speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws banning 'genocide ideology' and 'divisionism' as limits on speech
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has created numerous laws to prevent Rwandans from promoting a "genocide ideology" and "divisionism," with officials asserting such prohibitions are necessary for national unity and to prevent future genocide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes these laws are often used to prohibit government criticism and restrict speech; it also highlights that the laws' vague or broad scope enables prosecution or sanction for many forms of expression, and that the law does not always explicitly define the prohibited concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory definition of 'divisionism'
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisionism is defined in law as 'the use of any speech, written statement, or action that divides people, that is likely to spark conflicts among people, or that causes an uprising which might degenerate into strife among people based on discrimination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that the definition is broad and that it does not require that one's beliefs be spoken; this vagueness contributes to uncertainty and self-censorship because ordinary speech can be construed as divisionist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadly defined limits and discretionary enforcement by police/authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The country's broad definition of the limits of free speech has allowed police to make their own interpretations of the law and exile journalists as the government pleases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This discretionary enforcement is described as creating an environment where officials can selectively interpret statutes to target critics, contributing to media restrictions and press license revocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist licensing requirement (RURA) and license revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rwandan journalists are required to obtain licenses from the government-controlled Rwanda Utilities Regulatory Authority (RURA); Article 34 plus bans on genocide ideology and divisionism have commonly been used to revoke journalists' licenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives examples of outlets whose licenses/operations were blocked (Inyenyeri News, The Rwandan, Le Prophete) and cites Committee to Protect Journalists reporting that threats and possible jail sentences cause journalists to self-censor beyond official limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking and shutdown of media outlets (including international ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities have blocked or shut down media outlets (domestic and foreign) that are seen as critical or 'revisionist' (example: Rwanda shut down BBC locally after a documentary on the genocide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate operational measures (blocking, shutdown) used in practice. The guidance conveys that such actions are often justified by references to genocide-related offences or national unity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation of self-censorship among journalists and civilians
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear of possible legal ramifications from breaking broadly defined speech laws has led to a culture of self-censorship among both civilians and the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Committee to Protect Journalists and other sources are cited to show that threats, potential jail sentences, and license revocations cause journalists to avoid topics the government might construe as critical or divisionist, extending censorship beyond direct state action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control of education and historical narrative about the genocide
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-genocide, government-approved history textbooks stress Rwandans as 'one people' and largely ignore ethnic differences and pre-genocide conflicts; the 2016 curriculum change aimed for more balanced discussion but remains limited by divisionism/genocide ideology laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers reportedly fear repercussions for non-approved discussions and therefore self-censor, limiting students' exposure to fuller accounts of the genocide. This is presented as an institutionalized form of information control in education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political-information controls: prosecution, imprisonment, exile and alleged assassinations of opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: The government has threatened, imprisoned, and prosecuted journalists and political opponents (examples: Victoire Ingabire, Diane Rwigara); there are also reports and rumors of assassinations of exiled opponents (examples: Patrick Karegeya, André Kagwa Rwisereka).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames these practices as methods to eliminate political dissent, especially around elections. Legal prosecutions invoke charges such as 'conspiracy against the country' or 'genocide denial,' illustrating the use of criminal statutes to silence opponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempts to regulate social media for politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2017 the administration attempted to create rules requiring government approval of all social media by politicians to prevent opposition candidates from 'poisoning the minds' of Rwandans; after international backlash the policy was not enacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as an example of proposed top-down information controls aimed at political messaging; even unsuccessful proposals indicate the government's inclination toward regulating political speech online.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical justification for restrictive media laws (preventing radio-style incitement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to radio broadcasts' role in encouraging the 1994 genocide, Rwanda's government imposed strict guidelines on speech and press related to the genocide and Hutu/Tutsi ideologies; Kagame defended these laws as necessary for national unity and preventing future genocide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article acknowledges the stated rationale for restrictions (preventing recurrence of violence) while documenting critics' concerns that the measures are used to ban government criticism and limit free expression more broadly.
